protections: Reject prototype-mutating keys (__proto__, constructor, prototype) wherever a caller- or payload-supplied key is written into an object; in the pinned tree this guard exists only in parse_str (src/php/strings/parse_str.js:77).
Never write a fixed property through a prototype-chain lookup keyed by a caller-supplied name (src/php/info/ini_set.js:17-19,42).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: A prototype-pollution guard is already present at parse_str.js:77 and every parameter name passes through it, so the file reads as fixed.
array_merge returns a fresh object, so writing '__proto__' can only change that object's own prototype and cannot reach Object.prototype.
The recursive merge copies into a fresh accumulator, so the '__proto__' descent ends on a newly created object and never on Object.prototype.
array_replace copies into a fresh object; the missing hasOwnProperty test reads as a PHP-semantics bug, not a security one.
The recursive call returns a new copy, so nothing shared is mutated; the recursion condition looks like ordinary replace logic.
unserialize builds fresh objects from text and PHP parity requires arbitrary string keys, so the keys read as data rather than as a security boundary.
ini_set is a configuration setter that developers call with literal names, and it is not the function named in the advisory.
array_change_key_case is a cosmetic renaming helper and callers are not expected to feed it JSON-parsed attacker keys.
The dangerous string comes from a value rather than a property name, and PHP keys must be scalars, so the path looks theoretical.
The key is a value taken from a caller-supplied key list, not a property name, so the write looks like ordinary PHP array construction.
Every one is a plain copy loop with an own-key or value test; they look like ordinary array plumbing rather than merge/parse code.

masking: array_merge_recursive decides the merge path with 'key in result' (array_merge_recursive.js:44); '__proto__' is already 'in' through Object.prototype, so the write is reached through the inherited-lookup branch, and changing that test to an own-property test alone would move the key to the plain assignment at line 57 while leaving the prototype write open.

parse_str's guard stops the whole parameter loop with 'break' (parse_str.js:77-79); a correctness fix that turns it into 'continue' re-enables every later parameter, so later dangerous names reach the traversal the break was hiding.

Once parse_str's string check is replaced by a post-normalization check, ordinary names such as 'a.b' still pass through keys[0] normalization (parse_str.js:116-121) and the same object walk (parse_str.js:150-157); the walk itself is the sink and is only visible once the string check is bypassed.

conflicts.what: Using an Object.create(null) accumulator is the obvious way to make array_merge immune, but array_merge_recursive's merge decision at line 44 answers through Object.prototype and callers expect a normal object; changing the accumulator type alters both merge decisions and returned-object behaviour, so the two sites need one shared key policy rather than independent accumulator changes.

A null-prototype accumulator for array_replace removes the truthy inherited-object path that array_replace_recursive tests at line 34 (retObj[p] is truthy for Object.prototype), so the fix in one file silently changes the recursion in the other.

Both are check-then-rename shapes; the safe rule is to re-check the key after normalization. In parse_str the rename (dot/space to underscore) is documented PHP behaviour that must keep working for ordinary names, so a blanket rejection of dotted names would fix T1 and break legitimate input that T8's callers rely on.

fairness_risks: parse_str already refuses any name containing 'constructor' or 'prototype' as a substring and stops parsing the entire string (parse_str.js:77-79); e.g. 'constructors=1&a=2' yields {}, so a security rule keyed on substrings contradicts legitimate field names.
PHP maps '.' and ' ' in the first name segment to '_' (parse_str.js:116-126); a rule that refuses dotted or spaced names to close T1 breaks documented request-parsing behaviour such as 'user.name=1'.

array_merge/array_replace/unserialize must keep accepting arbitrary string keys, including 'constructor', 'prototype' and '__proto__' as ordinary PHP array keys; filtering them changes documented array semantics and serialize/unserialize round-tripping (serialize.js:98-110 emits such own keys).

array_merge must keep renumbering numeric keys (array_merge.js:52-56) and array_change_key_case must keep returning arrays unchanged (array_change_key_case.js:23-25); a filter that skips non-numeric or renamed keys changes these results.

design.why: Five independent fix sites across four directories, each with a different dismissal. T1 is the how-type bypass that survives the existing parse_str guard (a check that runs before name normalization), so a solver who sees the guard stops there; T2 and T3 are absent guards with the strong 'fresh object' dismissal, one a parallel entry point and one a second merge implementation whose existence test reads through Object.prototype; T6 is a deserializer off the report's path whose keys look like data; T7 is the only non-parse_str route that actually reaches Object.prototype (a fixed property written through the value of an attacker-chosen name) and has the strongest dismissal because it is a config setter. The mix covers both blind spots: the how-type under-guarded check (MiMo) and absent routes with good reasons to dismiss (DeepSeek). It beats a parse_str-only design, which is a single check in one file, and beats the copy-family design (T11), which is many easy repetitions of one already-accepted concept.

If the later fix only rewrote parse_str's guard, only T1 is covered by hidden tests and this candidate collapses to a single-trap task (usable would then be no).

Global impact of T2/T3/T4/T5/T6 is limited in the pinned code to the prototype of the object or array each function returns (single-level assignment into a fresh accumulator); no path from those sites to Object.prototype was found, so any claim that they pollute Object.prototype itself is unverified.
T7's real-world reach requires an application to pass a request-derived name to ini_set; the code path is present (ini_set.js:17-19,42) but no advisory evidence ties it to GHSA-vc8f-x9pp-wf5p.
Distance values are directory/file hops estimated from the tree, not measured.
array_fill_keys (T9) and array_combine (T10) only set a prototype when the caller supplies a non-primitive value for the new key; whether a fix would cover value-as-key paths is unverified.
